chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
title: The segregated Cotton Club and Bill Robinson's way in
summary: Crawford says the club admitted no Black patrons except Bill Robinson, and entertainers who objected would be fired.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Now, the policy then was -- the Cotton Club was still a segregated place at that time, wasn't it?
Yes. Nobody came in there Black but

Bill Robertson. Bill Robertson, you know how he got in there. Tam his way in, (Inaudible) you know, that laugh. Somebody like Woogie Harris, who they knew had a lot of money. I don't know whether you know Woogie Harris.
That's all. That's all, to my knowledge. Maybe Ethel Waters, I don't know, but Bill Robertson, he was the only Black allowed in there.
Now, you say this is because he charmed his way in.
So how did -- did the Black entertainers in those days --
They couldn't -- they couldn't say nothing and better not or else they would be fired.
If they said anything about the policy.
Yeah, don't come in my club telling me how to run it. Who are you? Oh, they would (Inaudible) turn everything.
